questions.questionText: Why does linear regression minimize squared error rather than, say, the raw (signed) error?
options: Squared error is faster to compute
Squaring makes all errors positive (so they don't cancel) and penalizes large errors more heavily
Squared error is only used for classification
questions.correctAnswer: Squaring makes all errors positive (so they don't cancel) and penalizes large errors more heavily
questions.explanation: If you summed signed errors, a +10 and a -10 error would cancel out to look like a perfect fit. Squaring fixes that and disproportionately punishes large misses.

questions.questionText: You set the gradient descent learning rate way too high. What's the most likely symptom?
options: The cost oscillates wildly or increases — the model diverges
Nothing changes, learning rate only affects speed
The model becomes immune to outliers
questions.correctAnswer: The cost oscillates wildly or increases — the model diverges
questions.explanation: A learning rate that's too large causes each update to overshoot the minimum, and the cost can bounce around or blow up instead of settling.

questions.questionText: What does a learned weight (coefficient) in linear regression represent?
options: The probability that the feature matters
How much the prediction changes for a one-unit increase in that feature, holding others fixed
The correlation between the feature and every other feature
The order in which features were added to the model
questions.correctAnswer: How much the prediction changes for a one-unit increase in that feature, holding others fixed
questions.explanation: This direct interpretability — each weight is a concrete "units of y per unit of x" — is one of linear regression's biggest practical advantages over black-box models.
